overview: F4104 combines formation emergency support with dynamic maneuvering. Students should be able to brief an airborne landing gear inspection, distinguish knock-it-off from terminate, execute cruise maneuvering with pursuit geometry, and explain the lead principles that keep Wing predictable and safe.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: A landing gear inspection is an emergency-support task, not a formation proficiency stunt. The inspection is flown only when it can be done without adding risk.

children.text: The aircraft with the unsafe indication notifies the other aircraft and ATC.
Climb to the published emergency orbit, delta pattern, or other local procedure before troubleshooting.
Request an airborne gear inspection if it will help the decision and can be done safely.
Wing follows the distressed aircraft and assists as directed.
Conduct the inspection at a minimum of 2000 ft AGL.
Use a discrete frequency when practical to reduce chatter and confusion.
The emergency aircraft communicates configuration, airspeed, altitude, and planned changes.
The inspecting aircraft reports position and intentions and avoids undue risk.
Use caution if visible damage could allow gear parts to depart the aircraft.
Student solos shall not join up to inspect landing gear.
Students shall not be at the controls during the landing gear inspection.
The emergency aircraft may ask Wing, chase, base, or RDO to help read checklists and troubleshoot.

items.text: Knock-it-off stops the maneuvering because safety is compromised or could be compromised.

children.text: Any flight member may initiate knock-it-off.
Use it for emergencies, traffic conflicts, blind situations, G-LOC or AGSM failure, area boundary concerns, or any developing unsafe condition.
The pilot calling knock-it-off should state the reason if able.
Lead maneuvers predictably, normally straight-and-level or with shallow bank.
Lead gives directive intentions and may state altitude and a reference heading for the flight.
Both aircraft prioritize separation and aircraft control before resuming any training objective.

items.text: Terminate stops an exercise or maneuvering for an expected or administrative reason; it is not the same as knock-it-off.

children.text: Lead normally initiates terminate, but Wing may request or initiate it.
Use terminate when the training objective is complete, the exercise is ending, or continuing would not be useful.
If the reason is safety-of-flight, call knock-it-off instead.
Lead remains predictable and transitions to a safe attitude.
Lead directs follow-on intentions, such as cleared to parade, continue, repeat, or recover.
Wing maintains deconfliction and does not rush the rejoin.

items.text: Cruise maneuvering teaches Wing to maintain position with pursuit geometry and lift-vector placement, not constant power chasing.

children.text: Lead signals cruise and holds a stable platform until Wing is established.
Wing acknowledges, slides to the 60-degree bearing line, sets the directed power, and calls ready.
Formation FTI references use about 80% torque above 10,000 ft and 70% torque below 10,000 ft before maneuvering; hold the PCL position rather than chasing torque changes with altitude.
Cruise position is about 60 degrees bearing, about 20 ft step-down, and 3 to 6 plane widths of spacing.
Lead is limited to no more than 120 degrees AOB and no less than 1G.
Wing uses lead, lag, and pure pursuit plus lift-vector placement to stay in the cruise cone.
Minor turns may need small power corrections; aggressive turns should be solved primarily with pursuit geometry.
Lead or Wing calls terminate.
Lead rolls level or establishes a predictable 30-degree AOB turn, stabilizes near 200 KIAS, and clears Wing to parade.
Wing maintains cruise spacing, anticipates acceleration or deceleration, and rejoins without losing step-down.

items.text: The principle of lead is to create a safe, predictable training platform while still meeting mission and area requirements.

children.text: Lead makes smooth, stable, predictable changes in power, heading, and altitude.
Lead keeps the flight within the assigned area and complies with current course rules or clearances.
Lead maintains cloud and traffic clearance unless operating on an IFR clearance.
Lead always knows Wing's position and monitors Wing's energy, aspect, range, closure, heading crossing angle, and line of sight.
Formation tasks take longer than single-ship tasks, so Lead must plan turns, radio changes, checks, and rejoins early.
Lead must understand area boundaries, wind effects, and how maneuver combinations affect ground track.
Lead should manage sun position and avoid forcing Wing to stare through Lead into the sun when practical.
A tight, abrupt maneuver has little training value if Wing cannot safely maintain position.

items.text: Lag and pure pursuit describe where Wing points the nose relative to Lead's flight path, which controls spacing and closure.

children.text: Lead pursuit points the nose ahead of Lead's flight path and decreases nose-to-tail separation.
Pure pursuit points the nose at Lead and shows little or no line-of-sight movement; closure initially exists but reduces as fuselages align.
Lag pursuit points the nose behind Lead's flight path and maintains or increases nose-to-tail separation.
In cruise maneuvering, Wing uses short lead or lag corrections, then returns toward the 60-degree bearing line.
Do not camp at Lead's 6 o'clock; closure is difficult to judge there.
In vertical maneuvering, standard cruise checkpoints may disappear, so preserving step-down is critical.
Supplement technique: compare the inboard horizontal-stabilizer tip to the fuselage star; stab tip on star is pure, stab tip forward of star is lag, and star forward of stab is lead.

studyNotes.summary: F4104 is a formation support and maneuvering event: inspect gear only with disciplined risk control, stop training correctly, and use pursuit geometry to manage cruise maneuvering.

summary: F4104 covers landing gear inspection support, knock-it-off and terminate calls, cruise maneuvering, lead principles, and pursuit geometry.
title: Landing Gear Inspection
